usage: everyday word for 'wow, cool!' when something is new or surprising in a good way
반말, the reaction you blurt out staring at something new
polite, mild wonder at something you just learned or saw
신기하다 + 거(것); 신기한 거 봤어 = I saw something cool
examples: 한국 지하철은 진짜 잘 돼 있어서 신기해요.
The Korean subway is so well-organized, it's amazing.
common reaction foreigners share with Korean friends
어? 이게 자동으로 켜지네. 신기하다.
Huh? This turns on automatically. That's cool.
혼잣말 muttered while poking at a gadget
눈 처음 봤을 때 너무 신기했어.
When I saw snow for the first time it was so amazing.
past tense 신기했어, recalling a first experience
nuance: 신기하다 is the go-to word for delighted wonder at something new, clever, or unexpected, like a smart gadget or your first snow. It carries a positive, almost childlike curiosity. Don't confuse it with 이상하다, which means weird in a slightly negative or off way.
mistakes: Using it for creepy/bad weirdness; that's 이상하다, not 신기하다 (신기하다 is positive wonder).
Writing 신기다 — the dictionary form keeps 하: 신기하다, 신기해요.

usage: for a view, music, or moment so beautiful you almost lose yourself
반말, said softly while taking something gorgeous in
황홀한 + noun; classic for sunsets, night views
황홀하다 + ㄹ 정도로 = so beautiful that...
examples: 남산에서 본 야경이 진짜 황홀했어요.
The night view from Namsan was truly mesmerizing.
강조 with 진짜, sharing a date highlight
벚꽃 길을 걷는데 황홀하더라.
Walking the cherry blossom path, it was just breathtaking.
-더라 recalling a vivid impression
공연이 너무 황홀해서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
The show was so enchanting I lost track of time.
-아서 cause; pairs with 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어
nuance: 황홀하다 describes beauty so intense it nearly sweeps you away, reserved for sunsets, night views, music, or a magical moment, not everyday 'pretty'. It feels literary and heightened, so dropping it on a so-so view sounds over the top. For ordinary 'pretty/nice' stick with 예쁘다 or 멋지다.
mistakes: Overusing it for mildly nice things; 황홀하다 is reserved for truly stunning, almost overwhelming beauty.
Confusing it with 행복하다 (happy); 황홀하다 is about being dazzled by beauty, not general happiness.

usage: the rush when you almost got hurt or look down from a height
반말 reaction right after a near-miss
past tense, retelling a scary moment
it's dizzying just to think about it
fixed phrase for 'I shudder to imagine'
examples: 차가 갑자기 끼어들어서 진짜 아찔했어요.
A car cut in suddenly and it was really heart-stopping.
near-accident on the road, very common
전망대에서 아래 보니까 아찔하더라고.
When I looked down from the observatory it made me dizzy.
-더라고 sharing a sensation; height-induced
하마터면 지갑 잃어버릴 뻔했어. 아찔해.
I almost lost my wallet. That was scary-close.
pairs with 하마터면...뻔했어
nuance: 아찔하다 captures the dizzy, stomach-dropping jolt of a near-miss or a dangerous height, the physical wave of 'whew, that was close'. It's both literal dizziness and the emotional shock of almost-disaster, so Koreans use it constantly after close calls in traffic. Don't swap it for 무섭다 (scary), which is steady fear rather than that split-second lurch.
mistakes: Using it for ongoing fear; 아찔하다 is a momentary dizzy jolt, not sustained 무섭다.
Saying 아찔하다 for happy excitement; it implies danger or vertigo, not fun thrill (use 짜릿하다).

usage: the cold shiver when something is eerie or menacing
반말, reacting to a horror scene or unsettling sight
past tense, retelling an eerie moment
섬뜩한 + noun; common with 느낌, 분위기
examples: 밤에 혼자 그 골목 지나가는데 좀 섬뜩했어.
Walking through that alley alone at night was a bit creepy.
very natural; 좀 softens it
그 사람 눈빛이 진짜 섬뜩하더라.
That person's stare was really chilling.
-더라 for a vivid impression of someone
뉴스 보다가 섬뜩한 사건을 봤어요.
I saw a chilling incident while watching the news.
섬뜩한 modifying 사건 (incident)
nuance: 섬뜩하다 is the cold-spine, hair-raising creepiness of something eerie or sinister, a dark alley, an unsettling stare, a disturbing news story. It's sharper and colder than 무섭다, focusing on that sudden chill rather than general fear. Reserve it for genuinely unsettling, spooky things, not everyday nervousness.
mistakes: Using it for ordinary fear of, say, exams; 섬뜩하다 implies eerie, spine-chilling dread.
Confusing it with 신기하다; 섬뜩하다 is negative and creepy, not fascinating wonder.

usage: covers both an awkward mood and an upset stomach
this feels awkward / my stomach's off
to feel queasy in the stomach
for a tense, awkward social atmosphere
examples: 과식했더니 속이 좀 거북해요.
I overate, so my stomach feels a bit queasy.
extremely common after a big meal
그 자리가 너무 거북해서 일찍 나왔어.
That gathering was so uncomfortable that I left early.
-아서 cause; awkward social setting
솔직히 그 질문은 대답하기 거북했어요.
Honestly, that question was awkward to answer.
V-기 거북하다 = awkward/uncomfortable to do (대답하기 거북하다)
nuance: 거북하다 has two everyday uses: a queasy, heavy stomach (속이 거북하다) and an awkward, uneasy social feeling. Both share the idea of something not sitting right, physically or emotionally. It's milder and more inward than 불편하다, which leans toward physical inconvenience, so use 거북하다 when you feel subtly ill-at-ease.
mistakes: Using it only for physical inconvenience like a hard chair; that's 불편하다 (거북하다 is queasy/awkward).
Forgetting the stomach sense; 속이 거북하다 is a super common natural collocation.

usage: to feel let down by someone's coldness
soft resentment when someone you care about is unkind or distant
반말, gentle reproach to a close person
-더라 recalling a moment you felt slighted
examples: 힘들 때 연락 한 번 없어서 좀 야속했어.
You didn't reach out once when I was struggling, it felt cold.
classic use toward a friend
바쁜 건 알지만 그래도 야속하더라고.
I know you were busy, but still, it felt heartless.
-더라고 sharing a hurt feeling
날씨까지 야속하게 비가 오네요.
Even the weather is being cruel, it's raining.
playful use; blaming circumstances
nuance: 야속하다 is the soft, wounded resentment you feel when someone close lets you down or seems cold, less anger than quiet hurt. It implies you expected warmth and didn't get it, so it carries affection underneath the complaint. It differs from 섭섭하다 (which is broader disappointment) by emphasizing the other side's seeming heartlessness.
mistakes: Using it for strangers; 야속하다 implies you expected kindness, so it fits close people or fate.
Treating it as strong anger; it's gentle, hurt reproach, not 화나다.

usage: the cozy warmth of a homey scene or close relationship
adverb form; 정겹게 인사하다 = greet warmly
examples: 시장에 가면 사람 사는 게 느껴져서 정겨워요.
At a traditional market you feel real life, it's so heartwarming.
very natural sentiment about 시장
할머니 댁은 늘 정겨운 냄새가 나.
Grandma's house always has a cozy, homey smell.
정겨운 modifying 냄새
오랜만에 만났는데 정겹게 안아줬어요.
We hadn't met in ages and they hugged me warmly.
정겹게 adverb with 안아주다
nuance: 정겹다 carries the uniquely Korean feeling of 정 (deep affectionate warmth), the cozy, homey heart you get from a traditional market, an old neighborhood, or a close-knit gathering. It's about human warmth and connection, not just physical comfort. Being a ㅂ-irregular adjective, it conjugates 정겨워요, 정겨운, so practice those forms.
mistakes: Conjugating it regularly as 정겹어요; it's ㅂ-irregular, so it's 정겨워요, 정겨운.
Using it for cute objects; 정겹다 is about heartfelt human warmth, not 귀엽다.

usage: the aching fondness of longing or cherished love
반말, reacting to a touching story or memory
애틋한 + noun; common for couples or family
fixed phrase for deep affectionate feeling
examples: 첫사랑 얘기를 하니까 표정이 애틋해졌어.
When they talked about their first love, their face turned tender.
애틋해지다 = grow tender
멀리 떨어져 있으니까 더 애틋해요.
Being far apart makes the feeling even more tender.
long-distance relationship context
부모님 사진을 보면 애틋한 마음이 들어요.
Looking at my parents' photo brings a tender, longing feeling.
애틋한 마음 + 들다
nuance: 애틋하다 is a tender, bittersweet fondness, the ache of cherishing someone you miss or love deeply, often tinged with longing or distance. It's gentler and more wistful than plain love, carrying a touch of melancholy. Use it for first loves, family far away, or any precious bond you hold close in your heart.
mistakes: Using it for casual liking; 애틋하다 is deep, bittersweet tenderness, not light 좋아하다.
Confusing it with 안타깝다 (pity for misfortune); 애틋하다 centers on tender longing.

usage: for blurry distant memories or a dreamy, faint impression
아련한 + noun; super common with 추억
adverb; 아련하게 떠오르다 = come faintly to mind
examples: 어릴 때 기억이 이제 좀 아련해요.
My childhood memories are kind of hazy now.
natural for fading memories
그 노래 들으면 옛날 생각이 아련하게 나.
When I hear that song, old memories come back faintly.
아련하게 + 나다 (생각이 나다)
사진 속 풍경이 아련해서 더 그리웠어요.
The scenery in the photo was hazy, making me miss it more.
-아서 linking to 그립다
nuance: 아련하다 describes something faint and hazy, especially distant memories that blur at the edges, leaving a soft, wistful longing. It blends 'dim/unclear' with gentle nostalgia, so it almost always pairs with 추억 (memories) or 생각. It's dreamier than just 흐릿하다 (blurry), because it carries that bittersweet pull of the past.
mistakes: Using it for physically blurry vision; that's 흐릿하다 (아련하다 carries nostalgia).
Applying it to clear, recent events; 아련하다 needs that faded, distant quality.

usage: the chest-swelling satisfaction after an accomplishment
반말, the warm glow after doing something well
past tense, recalling a satisfying moment
examples: 드디어 한국어로 주문에 성공해서 너무 뿌듯했어요.
I finally managed to order in Korean, I felt so proud.
relatable win for a learner in Korea
월급 받으니까 진짜 뿌듯하다.
Getting my paycheck feels really rewarding.
혼잣말, satisfaction after hard work
방 청소 다 하고 나니까 뿌듯해.
After finishing cleaning my room, I feel fulfilled.
-고 나니까 = after doing, then...
nuance: 뿌듯하다 is the warm, chest-swelling pride and fulfillment you feel after accomplishing something, finishing a task, hitting a goal, or doing a small thing well. It's inward satisfaction, not bragging, so it's modest and very common in daily life. Unlike 자랑스럽다 (proud of someone/something, often outward), 뿌듯하다 is the quiet glow you feel inside.
mistakes: Using it to mean 'proud of someone else'; that's usually 자랑스럽다 (뿌듯하다 is your own inner fulfillment).
Spelling it 부듯하다; it's the tense consonant: 뿌듯하다.

usage: the bashful awkwardness after a small misstep or being caught
겸연쩍은 + noun, common with 표정, 미소
examples: 이름을 잘못 불러서 겸연쩍었어요.
I called the wrong name, so I felt sheepish.
minor social slip-up
칭찬받으니까 겸연쩍게 웃었어.
When I got complimented I laughed sheepishly.
겸연쩍게 adverb with 웃다
혼자 김칫국 마신 게 좀 겸연쩍더라.
Getting my hopes up for nothing felt a bit embarrassing.
-더라; pairs with idiom 김칫국 마시다
nuance: 겸연쩍다 is that mild, sheepish embarrassment when you've made a small slip or feel awkwardly self-conscious, like an apologetic, bashful smile. It's softer than 창피하다 (full embarrassment) and overlaps with 멋쩍다, but stresses a slightly guilty, apologetic shade. You'll often hear 겸연쩍게 웃다 for an awkward little laugh.
mistakes: Using it for deep shame; 겸연쩍다 is mild sheepishness, not strong 창피하다.
Spelling it 겸연적다; the ending is the tense 쩍다: 겸연쩍다.

english: having a clear conscience, upright, unashamed
usage: to be upright / have a clear conscience
confident you've done nothing wrong, nothing to hide
반말, standing by what you did
to feel guilty / unable to hold one's head up
negative form for a guilty conscience
examples: 난 잘못한 거 없으니까 떳떳해.
I didn't do anything wrong, so my conscience is clear.
standing your ground
떳떳하게 일해서 번 돈이에요.
It's money I earned through honest work.
떳떳하게 adverb modifying 일하다
거짓말한 게 있어서 떳떳하지 못했어요.
I had told a lie, so I couldn't feel at ease.
negative 떳떳하지 못하다 for guilt
nuance: 떳떳하다 means having a clear conscience, being able to hold your head up because you've done nothing shameful or dishonest. It's about moral confidence and integrity, often used as 떳떳하게 (openly, honestly) or the negative 떳떳하지 못하다 when you feel guilty. It's not mere bravery; it's the calm assurance of being in the right.
mistakes: Confusing it with 당당하다; 떳떳하다 stresses a clear conscience, while 당당하다 stresses bold confidence.
Spelling it 떳떳다 — keep the 하: 떳떳하다, 떳떳해요, 떳떳하게.
